subject: geography

moments.title: CFCs identified as ozone risk
moments.who: Mario Molina and F. Sherwood Rowland
moments.body: Molina and Rowland publish in Nature: chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) — used in refrigeration and spray cans since the 1930s — are stable enough to reach the stratosphere, where UV releases chlorine that catalyses ozone destruction. They later share the 1995 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with Paul Crutzen.
moments.takeaway: An apparently inert, useful chemical turned out to be doing global damage. The discovery was theoretical before the hole was directly observed.

moments.title: Antarctic ozone hole discovered
moments.who: Joe Farman and the British Antarctic Survey
moments.body: BAS researchers at Halley Station, having measured ozone since 1957, report a dramatic spring depletion over Antarctica. NASA satellite data had recorded the same signal but software had flagged the values as errors and discarded them. The hole was rediscovered in the data.
moments.takeaway: Long ground-based records caught what dramatic satellite imagery had missed — through automated quality control filters.

moments.title: Montreal Protocol
moments.body: 16 September 1987: the Montreal Protocol on Substances that Deplete the Ozone Layer is signed. CFCs and halons phased out. Subsequent amendments (London 1990, Copenhagen 1992, Beijing 1999, Kigali 2016) extend the controls to HCFCs and HFCs.

quote.text: Perhaps the single most successful international agreement to date.
quote.attrib: Kofi Annan, UN Secretary-General, on the Montreal Protocol

moments.takeaway: By 2016 the Kigali Amendment extended controls to HFCs (powerful greenhouse gases). All UN members have ratified — the first universally ratified treaty.

now.title: Recovery in progress
now.body: WMO Scientific Assessment of Ozone Depletion (2022): stratospheric ozone is on track to recover to 1980 values around 2066 over Antarctica, 2045 over the Arctic and 2040 over the rest of the world. The 2020-21 unusual Arctic ozone depletion shows recovery is non-linear.
now.open_questions: Why did Montreal succeed when climate negotiations have struggled? Answers include: clear single cause, substitute chemicals available, smaller economic stakes, and a problem visible in lifetimes.

reflection: Montreal is the model that climate diplomacy has tried to emulate. The key features — strong science, economic substitutes, universal participation, regular tightening — are easier to assemble for ozone than for fossil fuels.
